decided: A falsy `base` given to `joinURL` (`""`, `undefined`, `null`) is treated as `""`. The first segment that is kept then becomes the URL as written (Rule 2).
`joinURL` drops each segment after the base that fails `isNonEmptyURL`: `""`, `undefined`, `null` and exactly `"/"`. The base itself is never filtered (Rule 3).
`joinURL` strips one leading `"./"` or `"/"` from a segment and joins it with exactly one slash. Further leading slashes are kept (Rule 4).
`joinURL` does not resolve `..`. It appends such segments literally (Rule 6).
While the accumulated URL is still `""`, `joinURL` uses the segment as written, without stripping a leading `"./"` or `"/"` (Rule 5).
The joining slash comes from `withTrailingSlash(url)` (without query/fragment respect) followed by concatenation. When the base has a query or hash, the slash lands after it (Rule 7a).
`joinURL` keeps the last segment's trailing slash as written and adds or removes none (Rule 7).
`joinRelativeURL` drops only falsy inputs before choosing the prefix and trailing slash. A bare `"/"` stays in the input list (Rule 9).
`joinRelativeURL()` with no arguments follows the old `joinURL` path and returns `""` (Rule 10).
`joinRelativeURL` resolves `./` and `../` exactly as the old `joinURL` did, e.g. `joinRelativeURL("/a", "../b", "./c")` → `"/b/c"` (Rule 8).
The new `joinURL` replaces the old behaviour under that name. The old resolving logic moves to `joinRelativeURL`, and `joinURL` becomes a simple join (Rules 1–7).
`withBase` keeps calling `joinURL`, so an `input` containing `..` is no longer resolved against the base (Rule 12).
`joinRelativeURL` has no protocol, query or hash awareness. A protocol's `//` collapses to `/` and `?`/`#` are ordinary characters, as in the old `joinURL` (Rule 11).
